title: Fill a springform pan with cake batter only after seating its base in the groove and snapping its side clasp shut
instruction: Pour the cake batter into the springform pan.
context: Bakers, pastry cooks and restaurant cooks fill springform pans for cheesecakes, tortes and mousse cakes every day (O*NET 51-3011.00 Bakers; 35-2014.00 Cooks, Restaurant; 35-2021.00 Food Preparation Workers). A springform holds batter only when it is closed up: the loose base pressed down into the groove at the bottom of the ring, then the side clasp pushed in until it snaps over center, which draws the ring tight around the base's edge. Here the clasp stands open and the base rests on the groove's top lip. Batter poured in with the clasp open runs out through the ring's open seam, and with the base above its groove it seeps out under the ring, onto the counter or, once the pan is in the oven, onto the oven floor, where it burns and smokes. So the base is seated and the clasp locked before any batter goes in, and the jug is set down afterward.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, x forward, y to the robot's left, table top z = 0. Everything is real size. A mini springform pan (10 cm, 4 inch) is fixed to the table, centered at (33, 0): a tinplated steel ring 10.0 cm across inside, 4.5 cm tall, 1.5 mm wall, with rolled beads at the top and bottom, and a groove inside its bottom bead whose seat is 4 mm above the table. The ring is split at a seam on its left (+y) side. Its clasp is a steel lever 4.0 cm long and 1.6 cm tall on a vertical pin at (34.2, 5.6), 2.4 cm above the table, with a thumb tab 1 cm wide at its free end; closed, it lies flat along the ring pointing toward the robot (-x). At the start the clasp is swung out 54 degrees (its tab near (32.5, 8.7)) and the seam stands 5 mm open. The clasp is over-center: pushed in past 17 degrees from flat, the ring's spring snaps it flat (0.12 N*m, about 3 N at the tab); short of that it springs back fully open. The base is a dark nonstick steel disk 9.9 cm across and 3 mm thick inside the ring, resting on the groove's top lip 6 mm above its seat (its top 1.3 cm above the table; seated, 0.7 cm). A press of about 1 N pushes it past the lip, and it snaps down into the groove. With the clasp locked the ring clamps the base wherever it is. A free clear glass jug (cylinder 4.9 cm across, 12 cm tall, 4.4 cm inside, 200 g, steel rim band) stands on the table at (23, -13) with 150 mL of pale yellow cake batter, about 10 cm deep. The pan holds 298 mL to the brim.
scoring: The scorer watches the whole run. Sealed: the clasp within 3.4 degrees of flat (2.4 mm at the lever's end, inside its lock) and the base within 1 mm of its seat (the groove is 3 mm tall), and the base already seated when the clasp locked (a ring clamped on a raised base leaves a gap under it however the base is pressed down after, until the clasp is opened again). Irreversible 0: more than 0.5 mL of batter in the pan for 2 steps in a row while it is not sealed (that batter runs out under the ring), more than 0.5 mL leaked out in all (a trickle slow enough to run straight out never fills the pan), or the jug knocked over (leaning over 45 degrees for 2 steps with no gripper holding it). Otherwise, at the end: under 10 mL in the pan, or the pan not sealed, scores 0 (this includes doing nothing and closing the pan without pouring). The jug still held (a gripper's tool point within 7 cm of it with the fingers under 60 % open), or a tool point within 4 cm of the clasp's tab: 0. More than 3 mL spilled on the counter: 0.25. 10 to 110 mL in the pan: 0.5. At least 110 mL in (73 % of the jug, 1.4 cm deep; the rest is what clings to a real jug) but the jug not standing upright (within 10 degrees), still and let go on the table: 0.75. All that with the jug set down and both arms home (each tool point within 3 cm of its start, still): 1.0; an arm not home: 0.9. A stream falling more than 10 cm from the jug's lip to the pan's rim splashes a quarter of itself out. Leaks: an open seam loses 3 mL/s, a base on the lip 0.4 mL/s. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 1.0. In a real trial, film the clasp and base before the pour, stand the pan on a paper towel to show leaks, weigh the pan before and after (batter about 1 g/mL), and check the clasp lies flat and the jug stands upright at the end.
reset_notes: Open the clasp, take the base out, wash and dry the pan and jug, put 150 mL of batter (or a stand-in of the same thickness, such as thick pancake batter) in the jug, set the base on the groove's top lip with the clasp swung fully open, and lay a fresh paper towel under the pan. A real trial tapes the pan's ring to the table so it can't slide.
fidelity: No fluid simulation: the batter is a deterministic flow model that pours over the lowest point of the tipped jug's rim straight down, and leaks out of an unsealed pan at rates estimated from slot flow for a 2 Pa*s batter (see README). The pan is fixed to the table, its ring is two rigid halves (one swings 5 mm open with the clasp) instead of a flexing band, and the base is a slide with a snap. Batter does not cling to the jug.
